item.title: Denser Planar Color Codes
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Superdense 4.8.8 color code memory achieves distance d using q=(2d2+5d−5)/2 total physical qubits with a twelve-layer CNOT cycle. Requires asymptotically 2/3 as many qubits as triangular 6.6.6 color codes and 1/2 as many as rotated surface codes.

Grade 0.467 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · Noah Shutty

Figure

Logical error per cycle ℓ as a function of total physical qubits per logical qubit q/k under SI1000 noise at p=10−3 and p=5×10−4. Shows 4.8.8 color codes achieving lower logical error than 6.6.6 color codes and rotated surface codes for a fixed physical qubit footprint.

Asks

Can 4.8.8 color codes achieve lower total physical qubit overhead than 6.6.6 color codes and surface codes under circuit-level noise and ancilla costs?

Before

Data qubit overhead ratio n/(kd2) was 1 for rotated surface codes and 3/4 for 6.6.6 color codes (Bombin 2006, Landahl 2014), while 4.8.8 reached 1/2 without ancilla or circuit noise optimizations.

But

Circuit-level SI1000 noise model with native CZ gates at p=10−3 and p=5×10−4; planar triangular and torus codes with nearest-neighbor 2D square lattice connectivity.

Tools

Brickwork lattice embedding · Superdense syndrome extraction · Pauli frame tracking · Tesseract decoder · Stim circuit simulation

Abstract

We consider the 4.8.8 color code in a brickwork layout on the square lattice with nearest-neighbor gates. We identify periodic superdense circuits with twelve CNOT layers that appear to preserve the full distance of these codes. Including ancillas, the family uses q=(2d²+5d-5)/2 physical qubits for distance d: asymptotically 2/3 as many as the triangular 6.6.6 color code and 1/2 as many as the rotated surface code at the same code distance. Circuit-level simulations targeting superconducting architectures demonstrate favorable scaling of 4.8.8 color codes at plausible physical noise rates, including both for planar codes and their toroidal cousins under periodic boundary conditions.

item.title: The Pinnacle Architecture with fixed connectivity of degree eight
item.description:
Worth a look incremental — Pinnacle architecture achieves degree-8 fixed connectivity, factoring a 2048-bit RSA integer in one month using 120 820 physical qubits with logical error rate 1.4×10−18 per logical qubit per logical cycle at d=24.

Grade 0.433 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Paul Webster, Tom Peham, Lawrence Z. Cohen

Figure

Per-block logical failure rate plotted against code distance d for memory, shift, and bridged measurement operations at physical error rate p=10−3, comparing simulated small distances to fits extrapolated to d=24.

Asks

How does adapting the Pinnacle architecture to superconducting qubits with fixed fabrication connectivity affect physical qubit overhead?

Before

was under 100 000 physical qubits in a hardware-agnostic baseline architecture with reconfigurable connectivity (Ref. [13])

But

Simulations run on small distances d∈{4,6,10} and extrapolated via sub-threshold fit to d=24; assumes physical error rate p=10−3, 1 µs code cycle time, and 10 µs reaction time.

Tools

Frozen Pinnacle Architecture · generalized bicycle (GB) codes · gadget-based Pauli product measurement · cyclic shift automorphisms · CP-SAT scheduling

Abstract

We show how the Pinnacle architecture can be adapted to be compatible with superconducting qubits, where the connectivity between qubits must be fixed at fabrication. Specifically, we present a modified instantiation of the architecture that has fixed connectivity degree of eight. With this instantiation, we show that a 2048-bit RSA integer can be factored in one month with approximately 120 000 physical qubits, given a physical error rate of 10⁻³, code cycle time of 1 microsecond and reaction time of 10 microseconds.

item.title: Single-atom-based asynchronous photonic interconnect for scalable modular quantum computing
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Memory-assisted single-atom interconnect achieves linear scaling with photon delivery probability p~ , reducing the attempt rate required for a 104s−1 entanglement rate from 190MHz (type-II fusion) to 3.2MHz at p~=1% .

Grade 0.399 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Jérémy Raskop, Nadav Kandel, Yaniv Amichy, Yaron Jarach, Tal Kanonich, Andrei Militaru, Johannes Fink, Barak Dayan

Figure

Entanglement rate and performance metrics plotted against attempt rate and delivery probability, showing a nearly 60-fold reduction in required repetition rate to reach 104s−1 compared to type-II fusion.

Asks

How to scale entanglement rates between modular quantum processing units linearly with low single-photon delivery probabilities without requiring two-photon interference or simultaneous photon arrival?

Before

Linear-optics type-II fusion BSM gates scale quadratically as 0.5p2 and require simultaneous arrival of indistinguishable photons, needing an attempt rate Rbs≃190MHz at p~=1% for 104s−1 entanglement rate.

But

Infidelity budgets δ=1%–5% limit waiting window length due to unheralded photon-atom scattering and atom dephasing T‾2∗; excludes input state preparation errors, motional ground-state cooling downtime, and atom reloading.

Tools

trapped single ⁸⁷Rb atom in fiber Fabry–Perot microcavity · symmetric Duan–Kimble cavity reflection photon–atom CZ gate · dual-rail path encoding · Monte Carlo simulations

Abstract

Scaling quantum computation beyond the capacity of a single quantum processing unit requires quantum interconnects between modular processors. Optical photons are natural carriers for distributing entanglement between these processors. Most loss-resilient protocols use photonic Bell-state measurements based on the linear-optics type-II fusion gate. The resulting entanglement rate scales quadratically with each processor's typically low photon-delivery probability. Here we analyze a memory-assisted quantum interconnect using a near-deterministic, robust photon--atom controlled-Z gate via a single atom trapped in a high-finesse cavity. Detecting and measuring a photon from one processor heralds entanglement between that processor and the atom. This entanglement is preserved while the process repeats with the second processor until the second photon is detected and measured. Reading out the atomic qubit finalizes the entanglement between the processors. As the entanglement is mediated by the atom, the photons from both processors do not need to be indistinguishable, removing a major source of infidelity. Furthermore, by removing the simultaneous photon-arrival requirement, the protocol allows the entanglement rate to scale linearly rather than quadratically with photon-arrival probability over a wide parameter range. We derive entanglement rates under realistic parameters, accounting for decay of the atom's entanglement with the first processor and for decoherence caused by unheralded photon interactions. The nanosecond-scale of the gate and read-out operations leads to orders-of-magnitude entanglement-rate gain over linear optics, removing a key bottleneck in modular quantum computing.

item.title: Oracle Synthesis Based on X-Map Decision Diagrams
item.description:
Worth a look new method — X-Map decision diagram (XMDD) synthesis lowers 10-variable Boolean oracle gate costs to 16184 average T gates and 13791 CX gates, using at most one ancilla qubit.

Grade 0.398 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Xin Hong, Kezhen Zhang, Aochu Dai, Sanjiang Li, Shenggang Ying, Mingsheng Ying

Figure

Stacked bars show the percentage of test cases where XMDD uses fewer (green), equal (orange), or more (red) T gates compared to ESOP across variable counts n=2 through 10, reaching 100% better cases for n≥8.

Asks

Can decision diagrams combining local invertible maps and complement edges synthesize quantum oracles with fewer T and CX gates?

Before

Exclusive-Sum-of-Products (ESOP) averaged 38579 T gates and 32929 CX gates on the same 10-variable test suite; Qiskit required 10973 T gates and 9390 CX gates at 8 variables.

But

Evaluated on randomly generated Boolean functions up to 10 input variables; Python implementation compared against C++ ESOP tool and Qiskit.

Tools

X-Map decision diagrams · Shannon decomposition with complement edges · single ancilla branch activation · recursive circuit synthesis

Abstract

Quantum oracles act as reversible black-box operators that encode classical Boolean functions into quantum states, enabling efficient function evaluation in quantum superposition. The resource efficiency of oracle implementation is critical to the performance of numerous quantum algorithms. Most state-of-the-art oracle synthesis approaches rely on compact Boolean function representations such as exclusive-sum-of-products (ESOP), yet still suffer from excessive T-count and CX-count for large-scale functions. In this paper, we propose a novel compact representation named X-Map decision diagram (XMDD) for Boolean functions, which integrates local invertible maps and complement edges to achieve higher compression efficiency. Based on XMDD, we further develop an optimized quantum oracle synthesis algorithm. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that, for Boolean functions with more than seven input variables, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art ESOP-based approach and Qiskit in nearly all test cases, achieving simultaneous reduction in both T-count and CX-count without an obvious trade-off. Moreover, we show that the performance can be further boosted by employing more optimal variable orderings. The proposed XMDD-based framework provides a scalable and resource-efficient solution for practical oracle synthesis in near-term and fault-tolerant quantum computing.

item.title: Pauli-string grouping for VQE measurement reduction on a sparse-connectivity quantum annealer
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Only H2 embeds onto current quantum annealing hardware for VQE Pauli-string grouping; all other molecular instances exceed the 4800-qubit Zephyr Z12 graph by factors between 23 and 2.0×105, with BeH2 under full commutativity requiring at least a Z59 topology (>105 physical qubits).

Grade 0.396 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Raul Martinez, Miguel Sanchez-Beato, Mario Calonge

Figure

Compares grouping quality (number of Pauli groups) and computational cost (wall-clock time) for molecular Hamiltonians under full commutativity across classical heuristics and D-Wave solvers.

Asks

What is the physical-qubit embedding overhead, scalability limit, and practical performance of the Pauli-grouping colouring QUBO on a sparse-connectivity quantum annealer compared to classical heuristics?

Before

Small-scale colouring QUBO implementations on D-Wave processors exhibited rapid decay of valid samples with variable count (Jattana et al., 2023), but without characterizing the minor-embedding overhead or hardware graph capacity limits.

But

Evaluated on six molecular Hamiltonians in the STO-3G basis using Bravyi-Kitaev mapping and standard one-hot QUBO formulation. Compared against classical greedy heuristics rather than exact solvers.

Tools

D-Wave Advantage2_system1 (Zephyr topology) · D-Wave Leap Hybrid BQM solver · One-hot Minimum Vertex Colouring QUBO · Degree-counting minor-embedding lower bounds · Classical graph colouring heuristics (LF, RLF, Degree-Based)

Abstract

The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) requires a large number of measurements to evaluate molecular Hamiltonians. Expressing a molecular Hamiltonian as a linear combination of Pauli strings creates a measurement bottleneck: non-commuting Pauli strings cannot be measured simultaneously. Consequently, mutually commuting Pauli strings must be grouped and measured together to minimise the number of quantum-state preparations. This task maps to the minimum clique cover problem on a commutativity graph, an NP-hard problem typically addressed using classical heuristics. Although an Ising-model formulation has recently been explored on fully connected CMOS Ising machines and demonstrated on physical quantum annealers only at small scale, the embedding cost that governs its behaviour on hardware with sparse connectivity, where each logical variable must be represented by a chain of physical qubits, has not been characterised. In this work, we formulate the Pauli-grouping problem as a standard QUBO colouring model and study its scalability on a D-Wave quantum annealer. Across a series of molecular systems and for both qubit-wise and full commutativity, we quantify the growth in the number of logical variables and the QUBO interaction density, characterise the physical-qubit and chain-length overhead required for embedding on the Zephyr topology, and compare the annealer's time-to-solution and solution quality with those of heuristic classical baselines. This analysis identifies the threshold of molecular complexity beyond which hardware connectivity prevents viable embedding, and shows that a second, practical limit is reached earlier. The threshold therefore measures how far current annealers are from the regime in which pre-optimising a VQE measurement scheme on hardware would be worth considering.
